newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel under fire on past and future budgets.
newsitem.headline: Waigel under fire on past and future budgets.

text.p: Germany's Social Democrat (SPD) opposition launched a full-scale broadside on Wednesday against Finance Minister Theo Waigel, accusing him of violating the constitution and losing control of the budget.
The SPD said it would take Bonn to the constitutional court for breaching the 'golden rule' of state finance last year by letting the federal budget deficit exceed state investment.
And, after a meeting of the finance planning council, SPD regional politicians said "excessive" deficits in 1997 and 1998 could jeopardise Germany's chances of joining European monetary union (EMU).
Waigel replied Germany would hit the EMU deficit goal.
"From today's point of view, the public sector deficit will not exceed three percent of GDP in 1997," Waigel said in a statement after the meeting.

Speaking to the council, he said that despite "extremely difficult" circumstances he would limit federal borrowing next year to 58 billion marks -- a figure in line with planned state investment and make the 1998 budget conform with the constitution.

Launching the SPD legal protest, parliamentary party leader Rudolf Scharping said that in preparing the 1996 budget the government had misled parliament and violated the constitution by allowing the deficit to be higher than public investment.

"We are going to file a constitutional complaint," he told SWF radio. "The government already knew when it was planning the 1996 budget that new borrowing would exceed federal investment. That violates the constitution."
Scharping said the final federal deficit for 1996 was 78.3 billion marks, and investment just 61 billion marks.

The Finance Ministry dismissed the SPD's protest, saying prevailing legal opinion agreed that the constitution forbids planning a deficit above the level of investment, but not actually running a higher deficit. "The SPD complaint will fail," State Secretary Irmgard Karwatzki said.

Although the SPD legal attack could embarrass Waigel, it is unlikely to threaten his position for now since proceedings would probably be lengthy. Far more pressing are problems in drafting the 1998 budget and meeting 1997 fiscal targets.

In remarks to the finance planning council, which groups regional and local government, Waigel said economic growth would be too slow to cut high unemployment next year. The government also faces extra burdens of over 30 billion marks revealed by recent tax projections.

Waigel said that coalition negotiations on state finances for 1997 and 1998 were on schedule and constructive. He said the government would hold to its deadline for the cabinet to sign off on the 1998 budget on July 11.
But, after the council meeting, SPD-led federal states warned that Germany risked runaway budget deficits both in the current year and in 1998.
"For both 1997 and 1998 we fear there will be excessive current deficits and a further increase in the national debt," the majority of SPD-governed states said in a joint statement.
The SPD group also warned Germany might fulfil the Maastricht criteria on a "one-off" basis, but fail to meet the treaty's demand for lasting fiscal stability.

"Even if we manage to meet the criteria to join the third stage of EMU through one-off measures in 1997, the reference year, it is not certain now whether Germany will achieve sustainably stable finances," the statement continued.

No agreement was reached on creating an internal 'stability pact' to match the deal to enforce budget discipline under EMU at national level pushed through by Bonn at the recent European Union summit in Amsterdam. But a deal is likely this year.
